title: The role of consequence in evaluating approximate claims as true or false
description: Even when people know how accurate a claim of fact is, evaluating it as ‘true’ or ‘false’ is complicated given the imprecisions of natural language. How do people decide whether an approximate claim should be considered true or false? We test whether truth evaluations depend on the consequences of a claim’s approximation—i.e., whether the approximation caused something to happen that otherwise would not have happened. In Study 1 (N=880) and Study 2 (N=1130), participants were more likely to consider a claim false when its approximation was consequential. Study 3 (N=402), using a game with real monetary stakes, found that the strength of this effect depended on whether the consequences of a claim’s approximation were good or bad. These findings suggest that, even when people know exactly how well an approximate claim corresponds to the facts, truth evaluations depend on whether the claim’s approximation mattered in context.

title: Psychological Coupling: The Necessary Science of Human-AI Interaction
description: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly showing the potential to generate outputs with impact ranging from emotional support to belief distortion. However, a critical gap in AI safety research persists: current frameworks fail to capture how virtuous and maladaptive dynamics actually emerge through turn-by-turn conversational exchange. Building on dynamical systems research on human social interaction, we reframe human-AI exchanges as dynamic relational systems and introduce the notion of ‘psychological coupling’ as a candidate, empirically measurable mechanism driving psychosocial impacts from human-AI interaction. Providing the empirical foundation necessary to mitigate relational risks and actively promote adaptive, prosocial outcomes, this paper  further outlines the promises and challenges of a necessary shift from static safety benchmarks to empirical studies and longitudinal, simulation-based evaluations that capture these unfolding dynamic trajectories.

title: Compassion as a Mechanism for Intergroup Helping: Preliminary Evidence from a Humanitarian Education Intervention Across Six Non-WEIRD Countries
description: Compassion, the feeling of concern for a suffering other, accompanied by the motivation to help, is theoretically central to prosocial behaviour across group boundaries, yet evidence from non-WEIRD and conflict-affected settings remains scarce. This paper presents three exploratory lab-in-the-field studies of a socio-emotional learning (SEL) intervention grounded in Humanitarian Principles and Values. Exploratory Study 1 was implemented across four non-WEIRD countries (Armenia, Belarus, The Gambia, and Russia; n = 96 adolescents and young adults). Overall effects of the SEL intervention on social emotions or prosocial behaviour were not detected. However, intervention-induced increases in compassion predicted greater willingness to help out-group members, identifying compassion as a candidate mechanism linking humanitarian education to intergroup prosocial behaviour. Exploratory Study 2 (Appendix B) reports a feasibility study of a condensed one-day intervention in Zambia (n = 21), including a six-month follow-up on resilience and loneliness. Exploratory Study 3 (Appendix C) reports a feasibility study of a two-day intervention in South Sudan (n = 43), including a six-month follow-up on resilience and loneliness. Together, these feasibility studies extend the methodology to sub-Saharan and conflict-affected East African contexts. Both studies confirmed the methodological feasibility of the SEL intervention and the viability of longitudinal follow-up in resource-constrained contexts.

title: What Should Be Spaced? Variability Constrains Spacing Effects in Classroom Learning
description: The present study examined whether the effectiveness of spaced practice in authentic K–12 classrooms depends on the variability of instructional materials. Data were collected from 52 classrooms, including 1,050 middle and high school students across multiple subjects. Results showed that spaced practice improved long-term retention when practice repeatedly targeted the same item, even when questions varied in format. In contrast, spacing benefits were attenuated when practice involved different items aligned with the same instructional standard. Spaced practice also produced a modest benefit for transfer to novel items regardless of variability. These findings suggest an important boundary condition of spacing effects: the benefits of spacing depend on the extent to which practice opportunities preserve overlap that supports retrieval of prior learning. More broadly, the results refine theoretical accounts of spacing by highlighting potentially distinct mechanisms underlying retention and transfer and provide practical guidance for implementing spaced practice in educational settings.

title: Carpe diem or memento mori – The relationship between existential anxiety and temporal discounting
description:
This thesis investigates the relationship between existential anxiety and temporal discounting, which is the tendency to prefer smaller, immediate rewards over larger, delayed ones. The primary objective was to examine how inducing thoughts of one’s own mortality (mortality salience) influences impulsivity in financial decision-making. The theoretical framework is based on Terror Management Theory (TMT) and Paul Tillich's concepts of existential anxiety.
Method: An online study was conducted with 224 participants aged 18 to 72. Participants were randomly assigned to one of three groups: experimental (mortality salience), comparison (thoughts of physical pain at the dentist), and control (current emotional state). Tools used included the 5-trial adjusting delay task to measure the discounting rate (parameter k), the Existential Anxiety Questionnaire (EAQ), and the Purpose in Life Test (PIL).
Results: Statistical analyses did not support the primary research hypotheses. No significant differences in discounting rates were found between the mortality salience group and the control groups. Furthermore, existential anxiety levels and declared religiousness did not significantly correlate with the discounting rate of future gains. However, it was noted that higher levels of mindfulness (attention) during the study were associated with lower impulsivity (slower discounting). A strong negative correlation between existential anxiety and purpose in life was also observed.
Conclusions: The lack of significant manipulation effects may result from the socio-economic diversity of the sample or the situational context, aligning with Life History Theory (LHT). The findings suggest that the link between mortality awareness and economic decisions is complex and may be moderated by an individual's resources and the specific type of threat.

title: Modality-Specific Consolidation Shapes Long-Term Retention in Statistical Learning
description: Individuals routinely learn patterns from sights and sounds, yet it remains unclear how memories of those patterns compare across senses over time. Statistical learning, the implicit detection and extraction of patterns from continuous input, has been documented across sensory modalities, but most work has focused on immediate learning in unisensory contexts. This study, using a within-subject design, directly compared 24-hour consolidation trajectories of auditory, visual, and audiovisual statistical learning. Twenty-six young adults completed three statistical learning tasks across auditory, visual, and audiovisual modalities. In each task, participants were exposed to a continuous stream of stimuli with embedded triplet patterns. Learning of these patterns was tested immediately after exposure and again 24 hours later. Across immediate and delayed tests, multisensory exposure yielded higher accuracy than unisensory exposure, demonstrating a robust multisensory-over-unisensory advantage. In contrast, only auditory statistical learning showed overnight gains, whereas visual and multisensory learning remained stable, suggesting a consolidation advantage for auditory input. Cross-task correlations, both at immediate test and for consolidation magnitudes, were weak, suggesting substantial modality-specific contributions to statistical learning. These findings provide the first evidence that multisensory input boosts long-term retention of learned patterns, and the consolidation of these patterns operates in a modality-specific manner.

title: Kawaii (Cute) Feelings and Gender in Japanese Young Adults: Relations with Communion and Gender-Role Attitudes
description: “Kawaii (cute) feelings” are positive affective responses with culturally specific meanings in Japanese and have often been linked to femininity. This study examined the relations of kawaii feelings with communion (stereotypically associated with femininity) and gender-role attitudes. An online questionnaire survey was conducted among 330 Japanese university students (124 men and 206 women; M = 19.76 years, SD = 1.81). Kawaii feelings were assessed across four targets: infants, baby animals, characters, and objects. Agency, a personality stereotypically associated with masculinity, was also assessed for comparison with communion. Multivariate analysis of covariance revealed that positive communion, negative communion, gender-role attitudes, and gender were associated with kawaii feeling. Higher levels of both positive and negative communion were associated with stronger kawaii feeling toward infants and objects, more egalitarian gender-role attitudes were associated with stronger kawaii feeling toward characters, and women reported stronger kawaii feeling toward baby animals and objects than men. Agency was not significantly associated with kawaii feeling. These results highlight the importance of considering culturally specific emotions to understand how gender norms are maintained and transformed in contemporary Japanese society.

title: Testing the Dual Representation Account of Memory for Trauma
description: The finding that a visuospatial intervention can decrease involuntary memories following a laboratory analogue of trauma, without altering voluntary memory, is a crucial source of support for the Dual Representation Account (DRA) of intrusive memories. In two pre-registered experiments using Bayesian sequential designs, we tested predictions derived from the DRA. In Experiment 1, we first aimed to replicate the functional dissociation between voluntary and involuntary memory after a visuospatial interference intervention, while matching retrieval conditions more closely than in previous research. Second, we tested the prediction that the effect of the intervention would be greater in an analogue trauma condition than a neutral control condition. Third, we tested the prediction that voluntary memory would be decreased in the trauma condition relative to the neutral condition. Finally, we hypothesized that measures of voluntary and involuntary memory would not be correlated across participants. Unexpectedly, the results indicated that the visuospatial intervention did not decrease involuntary memories and that measures of involuntary and voluntary memory were positively correlated. In Experiment 2, we focused specifically on replicating the effect of the visuospatial intervention on involuntary memories of a trauma film. We did not replicate this effect: results provided substantial Bayesian evidence against an effect of the intervention.  Overall, our findings provide evidence against the DRA as a viable theoretical account of intrusive memories, at least in the context of a laboratory analogue of trauma.

title: Pluralism within limits: How to make the idea of multiple NCC kinds useful
description: Recently, several authors have argued that the current impasse in consciousness science supports a pluralistic interpretation: the view that seemingly contradictory findings may both be valid because consciousness can be brought about in different ways, each sufficient to generate conscious experience. We analyze different versions of pluralism to determine under what conditions it offers a viable interpretation of consciousness science. We argue that viable pluralism requires a two-factor framework distinguishing general consciousness factors (mechanisms rendering contents conscious) from content encoding itself. Moreover, NCC kinds must be finite in number and systematically ordered to enable a unified scientific model. While pluralism enables testable hypotheses, significant ontological tensions arise: how can consciousness constitute a unified natural kind if realized by fundamentally distinct NCC kinds? Drawing on philosophy of science, we propose an alternative interpretation in terms of scientific rather than natural kinds. Our goal is not to advocate for pluralism, but rather, to critically examine its viability and implications. Based on this, we urge the field to engage more explicitly with the foundational assumptions that shape consciousness research.

title: Pupil-linked arousal: more than noradrenaline
description: The literature on pupil-linked arousal shows a pervasive bias: it often attributes findings to the noradrenergic locus coeruleus while overlooking other neuromodulatory systems. Here, we quantify the extent of this bias and emphasize that correcting it is essential for refining theoretical models and improving interpretability in this rapidly evolving field.

title: The effect of semantic similarity on re-learning of vocabulary in activation and inhibition deficit in aphasia
description: Semantic similarity between known items (e.g., cat/dog) can interfere with a speaker’s ability to name them. Recent studies have shown that this interference extends to the acquisition of new vocabulary in neurotypical adults. However, the influence of such similarity on long-term retention of relearned vocabulary in individuals with aphasia remains unknown. This study examines this issue in two individuals with lexical retrieval deficits, who nevertheless show distinct profiles: one has difficulty activating lexical items (activation deficit), the other inhibiting lexical competitors (inhibition deficit). Participants were trained for six weeks using blocks of semantically related, unrelated, and mixed items. Learning was assessed during training, immediately after training, one week after each training session during the training period, and finally, two, six, and sixteen weeks after the last training session. We found a detrimental effect of semantic similarity on long-term retention in the inhibition, but not the activation, deficit. This dissociation shows that semantic similarity interacts with processes of activation and selection in a manner predicted by theories of incremental learning in language production. With regard to clinical implications, we found that, similar to neurotypical learners, semantic similarity among items in a training set can hurt the long-term retention, but that this effect can be ameliorated by spreading the related items across different training blocks within a session.

title: The Adoption of Open Science Practices in Communication Research: Taking Stock of the Field in 2025
description: Five years after Dienlin et al.’s (2021) agenda-setting article explicitly called for communication research to adopt open science practices, this study systematically assesses the current state within the field. Through manual content analysis of articles published in 2025 across 20 leading communication journals, we evaluated the adoption of six Transparency and Openness Promotion (TOP) Research Practices provided by the Center for Open Science, namely study registration, study protocol, analysis plan, materials transparency, data transparency, and analytic code transparency. The results show limited adoption of TOP research practices in communication research. Sharing of research materials is done more frequently than other practices, yet its extent of transparency remains limited. Quantitative studies achieve higher transparency scores than qualitative studies. Critically, justifications for non-sharing of materials, data, or analytic code, as well as explicit reporting of deviations from preregistrations, are mostly absent, despite their importance for transparency and openness. We argue that voluntary adoption may be insufficient and discuss whether stricter enforcement mechanisms are needed to establish open science as a normative standard. By mapping the current implementation of open science practices, this study contributes to critical reflection on the reproducibility and credibility of communication research and informs the development of infrastructures to support greater transparency.

title: Goals, Predictions, Valence: A Model Comparison of Agency Emergence
description: The sense of agency (SoA), our feeling of control over actions and their environmental effects, has been explained through different theoretical models. This study compares three: the comparator model, proposing that SoA emerges from matching motor predictions to perceptual feedback, the ideomotor model, proposing that SoA emerges from monitoring goal achievement, and a self-serving bias model, proposing that SoA reflects self-attribution of positive and external attribution of negative outcomes. Participants performed a target-hitting task with manipulated visual feedback of positive or negative valence and rated their SoA on a subset of trials. The three models predict different SoA patterns based on motor activity appropriateness, goal achievement, and outcome valence. The ideomotor model best fit the empirical data, outperforming both alternatives, though outcome valence showed an additional influence on SoA. These findings question the role of motor-based predictions in SoA emergence and highlight goal achievement as a key determinant of SoA.

title: Learning words in diverse narrative contexts disrupts subsequent recall of their meanings
description: Recent research suggests that encountering words in varied narrative contexts may disrupt the earliest stage of learning (Hulme et al., 2023). The current experiments explore (i) how this diversity disadvantage changes over learning, and (ii) whether diversity primarily impacts encoding or subsequent recall. Adults (Experiment 1: N = 105; Experiment 2: N = 111) encountered novel words with invented meanings within narrative paragraphs across three days. Words were presented within one coherent narrative (low diversity) or across nine different narratives (high diversity). We replicated Hulme et al.'s (2023) results for word-form learning, finding moderate/strong evidence for null effects of diversity on word-form recall and recognition (Experiment 1), and speeded word-form recognition accuracy (Experiment 2), and only anecdotal evidence of a diversity benefit on response times. For word-meaning learning, Experiment 1 replicated the diversity disadvantage on word-meaning recall reported by Hulme et al. (2023; extreme evidence), but in Experiment 2 there was moderate evidence for a null effect on semantic feature recognition. Findings indicate that while narrative diversity does not strongly influence participants’ ability to encode or retain semantic features for new words, words learned in low-diversity conditions initially build more coherent contextually-bound representations that facilitate recall of semantic features.

title: Executive functions in people with Williams syndrome: a scoping review
description:
Introduction. Williams syndrome (WS) is a genetic neurodevelopmental disorder associated with mild to moderate intellectual disability and a distinctive cognitive profile characterized by relative strengths in language and visuospatial difficulties. People with WS are characterized by an atypical pattern of hypersociability, manifested as marked social disinhibition. While their neurobehavioral profile strongly suggests significant impairments in executive functions (EF), empirical findings remain heterogeneous. Therefore, this scoping review aimed to synthesize and map the existing literature on EF in people with WS.
Methods. Following the PRISMA-ScR framework, ProQuest, Scopus, Web of Science, EBSCOhost databases were searched. Inclusion criteria required empirical data published between 2000 and 2025 targeting EF assessments or interventions in genetically confirmed WS cohorts as a distinct group. A total of 85 documents were included.
Results. Included studies predominantly featured cross-sectional comparative designs, often with small sample sizes. Findings revealed impairments across all executive domains examined. EF was significantly associated with emotional, behavioral, social, and adaptive outcomes, suggesting a central role in everyday functioning. However, considerable methodological heterogeneity was identified across studies.
Conclusions. People with WS exhibit severe and generalized executive dysfunction, which plays a critical role in their emotional, behavioral and social adaptation. However, the scarcity of longitudinal data limits the understanding of executive developmental trajectories. Furthermore, limited intervention evidence highlights the need for future studies to clarify which specific executive components are most amenable to improvement.

title: Digital shadows in mental health map how LLMs simulate depression, anxiety, and stress through language and psychometrics
description: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used for mental-health support, yet few datasets characterise how prompting conditions shape LLMs' psychological and linguistic outputs. To fill this gap, we introduce Mental Health Digital Shadows (MHDS), a benchmark of 75,000 outputs from 15 LLMs in conversation, under human-shadow or LLM-assistant conditions. MHDS includes outputs generated by several model families (Grok, DeepSeek, Mistral, and Qwen) or providers (Microsoft, IBM, and OpenAI). Human shadows are conditioned on sociodemographic and personality traits alongside assessments of their depression, anxiety, and stress levels, based on the Depression Anxiety and Stress Scale-21 (DASS-21). MHDS incorporates DASS-21 psychometric scores and three types of natural language texts: (i) an item-by-item explanation of shadows' DASS-21 numerical scores; (ii) a list of words expressing feelings; and (iii) six topic-oriented open-ended replies addressing mental health topics (e.g., stigma, support, and AI psychologists). Validating MHDS across its two conditions identifies a tendency for human shadows to alter their linguistic replies and psychometric scores according to prompting conditions, a pattern reminiscent of human behaviour and absent in LLM assistants. Further validation against human data finds that LLMs can produce distress scores resembling the distribution of human populations. Hence, MHDS offers a psychometrically grounded resource for studying how LLMs can debate mental health conditions, with applications in NLP, AI safety, bias detection, and well-being AI support tools.

title: The Construct Validity of Automated Written Interview Competency Assessments
description: We report evidence on the construct validity of automated written interview competency assessments (AWI-CAs). Participants (N = 117) provided written responses to 12 open-ended interview questions designed to assess four behavioral competencies (Collaboration, Communication, Leadership, Critical Thinking) along with a neutral question. Responses were scored by a large language model (LLM) on an 11-point scale. Scores were substantially intercorrelated, including correlations with the neutral question, suggesting substantial common method variance. Accordingly, we partialled out the neutral-question score from each behavioral question. Principal axis factor analysis with varimax rotation yielded a three-factor solution: Communication and Leadership loaded on a common factor, whereas Collaboration and Critical Thinking formed distinct factors. In addition, the Communication/Leadership factor was primarily associated with Open-Mindedness, the Collaboration factor with Conscientiousness, and the Critical Thinking factor with verbal reasoning. Overall, these findings support the construct validity of automated behavioral interviews beyond a general response tendency.

title: Do action video gamers search better than non-gamers?
description: Studies have shown that action video gamers are better at visual search than non-gamers, but less is known about the specific ways in which gamers excel. We conducted an extensive set of experiments to examine whether and how gamers and non-gamers differ in their search performance. We used both simple, efficient feature search tasks and difficult, inefficient configuration search tasks, including search for game-style figures. In four of the experiments, we adopted a psychophysical staircase procedure to determine the minimal display duration or target-distractor color difference required for participants to find the target. In the other eight experiments, we measured response time and search efficiency for efficient as well as inefficient search tasks. This study is the first to use both staircase procedures and response time measures to give a comprehensive examination of group differences between gamers and non-gamers in various aspects of visual search behavior. We found only minimal evidence for superior search skills among gamers. Only in one of four cases did we find a gamer benefit in their perceptual threshold - gamers’ color discrimination exhibit a higher robustness against search difficulty. In one of four efficient searches did gamers respond marginally faster or switch faster. On the other hand, in one of four inefficient searches gamers actually suffered more from increased set size, suggesting a less efficient search than non-gamers. These findings call for more cautious consideration of the advantage of gamers in visual search.

title: Predictions and outcomes independently shape the subjective experience of regret
description: Humans have the capacity to feel a subjective sense of regret – a rather sophisticated emotion that involves counterfactual simulation of the options not pursued when we act and decide. Pathological levels of regret are also a hallmark of multiple psychiatric conditions. However, little is understood about how subjective feelings of regret connect to the learning and inference processes we use to make decisions – and how alterations in these processes may explain atypical regret experiences. Here, we modified a reward learning task to include sporadic probes for post-choice regret. Computational modelling revealed that subjective feelings of regret were connected to reward outcomes, but importantly, were also independently tied to evolving predictions about action values. This perspective explains how the subjective experience of regret could be generated from the building blocks of more basic representations used in learning and inference.

title: Best practices and pitfalls in multivariate pattern analysis of event-related potentials: A systematic review of preprocessing and analytical configurations
description: Multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA, decoding) has been increasingly used in event-related potential (ERP) research. This growing use reflects several advantages of decoding approaches, such as their ability to exploit high-dimensional spatiotemporal ERP features, detect subtle and distributed neural differences between conditions, avoid subjective electrode selection, and provide time-resolved insights into cognitive processing. However, decoding performance is highly sensitive to preprocessing choices and analysis settings, many of which are directly inherited from conventional ERP practices despite not always being optimal for decoding analyses. Evidence indicates that preprocessing steps can differentially affect univariate ERP measures and decoding outcomes. Similarly, decoding-specific analysis parameters, including classifier selection, trial construction strategies, overfitting control methods, cross-validation schemes, and evaluation metrics, can substantially shape decoding performance and its interpretation. Importantly, commonly used metrics such as accuracy and AUC, while practical and widely implemented in popular toolboxes, may introduce bias under conditions such as class imbalance, which are prevalent in ERP paradigms. Here, we present a systematic review of ERP decoding studies published between January 2021 and December 2025, providing a quantitative overview of prevailing preprocessing pipelines and decoding configurations. We integrate these results with empirical and methodological evidence to discuss the mechanisms, benefits, and potential risks associated with common analytical choices, highlighting key divergences between decoding-oriented and conventional ERP methodologies. Finally, we identify recurrent methodological pitfalls and offer practical recommendations aimed at improving transparency, reproducibility, and methodological validity in future ERP decoding research.

title: Thinking clearly about sampling and representation with the Total Survey Error Framework
description: Collecting a sample that represents the population of interest well constitutes a challenge across the social and behavioural sciences. Psychology in particular frequently relies on convenience samples—most notably students and, increasingly, online participants—with a tendency to either (implicitly) assume representativeness without substantive justification, or to acknowledge a lack of it only in passing. In contrast, researchers rarely engage with the actual implications for their inferences, which undermines the generalisability of psychological findings. Critically, representativeness must be defined with respect to variables relevant to the target of inference, rather than superficial demographic diversity. Here we present the Total Survey Error (TSE) framework as a methodological tool that systematically addresses the multifaceted sources of error—particularly those related to representation—that emerge throughout the research cycle. Although TSE originated in survey research, its principles are broadly applicable to any psychological study seeking inference from sample to population. We offer practical strategies for identifying, preventing, and mitigating representation errors to improve the credibility and generalizability of psychological research.

title: State of Social Cognition Research: Challenges, Future Directions, and Efforts Toward Consensus Building
description: Social cognition research has become a key area of cognitive science, producing a wealth of theories, methods, and empirical findings. However, the field faces significant challenges that constrain further progress and broader impact. These challenges include a lack of conceptual clarity as well as methodological and psychometric issues. Conceptually, there is substantial variation in how social cognition is defined, subdivided, and labeled, alongside a limited understanding of its basic structure. Methodologically, existing assessment tools often show shortcomings, including inadequate assessment and reporting of psychometric properties. Furthermore, sufficiently interactive paradigms are still scarce, and the clarification and experimental control of participants’ strategy use and underlying cognitive processes involved in task performance remain insufficient. As a group of early-career researchers and clinicians with a broad variety of backgrounds and research foci reflecting the thematic diversity of the field, we aimed to develop an overview of these issues and propose ways forward. We argue that progress requires both humility and courage: acknowledging our field’s theoretical fragmentation and methodological limitations, and embracing complexity through multimethod, interactive, and computational approaches. We further call for consensus-building initiatives, open science practices, and large-scale collaborative research to address these challenges and further advance our understanding of social cognition.

title: What Do We Know About the Effects of Artificial Intelligence in Education? A Second-Order Meta-Analysis
description: Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming increasingly integrated into education. However, fundamental questions about its effects remain unresolved, with existing meta-analyses differing substantially in reported effect sizes, moderators that amplify or attenuate these effects, and methodological quality. To synthesize the fragmented evidence base and examine sources of these variations, we conducted a preregistered second-order meta-analysis aggregating 45 meta-analyses (129 effect sizes) based on approximately 197,000 learners from prekindergarten through university. Three-level second-order meta-analyses showed that AI applications in education had a medium effect across educational outcomes. Effects were larger in more recent meta-analyses, in meta-analyses including tertiary-education students, and for general academic outcomes than for STEM performance outcomes. We did not find significant differences between AI applications. Methodological quality of meta-analyses did not explain variance in effects, but our assessment identified systematic quality deficits (e.g., regarding reproducibility and open science). Insufficient statistical power was common among the included meta-analyses. Overall, these findings advance a more differentiated understanding of the current state of research on AI in education, highlighting both the potential of AI and the limitations of the evidence base.

title: Putting Out Statistical Fires: Assessing Model Fit Using DHARMa Randomized Quantile Residuals
description: Regression models and statistical tests abound in the social sciences. But are any of these models actually correct? Evidence shows that most models in psychology, and likely other social sciences as well, are not assessed for mis-specification, which damages the reliability of psychological research. This tutorial paper aims to bridge this gap. The paper primarily showcases a generalized approach to model fit using randomized quantile residuals from the DHARMa package in R. The paper is also accompanied by a website which provides a variety of examples with simulated and real-world social science data (https://dharma-for-social-science.netlify.app/). The purpose of this paper and website is to educate social scientists, particularly psychologists, on how to assess model fit across a wide spectrum of models, which may improve the reliability of findings in the field.

title: Pro Environmental Attitudes, Emotions, and Donations After Playing an  Ecogame - The Role of Post Gameplay Reflection
description:
Background 
Video games are increasingly recognised as promising tools for environmental education 
because of their potential to positively influence environmental attitudes and behaviours at 
scale. However, while effects of persuasive games appear consistent, effect sizes are generally 
small. In the specific context of ecogames, which are game about environmental issues, more 
experimental investigations of their effects are needed. 
Objectives 
This study investigated whether structured post-gameplay reflection amplifies the effects of the 
persuasive ecogame Gibbon: Beyond the Trees on pro-environmental attitudes and pro
environmental behaviour. Besides, it sought to strengthen the empirical evidence on ecogames 
by using an experimental design, full-game playthroughs, and including an outcome measure 
that extends beyond self-reported attitudes. 
Methods 
After completing a full playthrough, participants were randomly assigned to one of three 
conditions that differed in the level of structured post-gameplay reflection (none, moderate, or 
substantial). The study used a pre-test/post-test design with an optional one-week follow-up, to 
examine changes in palm-oil-related attitudes, wildlife value orientations, generalized 
environmental attitudes, and affective reactions to gameplay. Pro-environmental behaviour was 
assessed through voluntary donations to environmental NGOs. 
Results and Conclusions 
On average, this study observed improvements in pro-environmental attitudes post-gameplay, 
alongside affective changes aligned with the game’s narrative. Further, participants showed 
substantial behavioural responses, donating nearly half of their compensation (1.951,80€ in 
total) to environmental NGOs. Post-gameplay reflection did not significantly moderate 
attitudinal changes or donation amounts, suggesting that well-received commercial ecogames 
with strong alignment between narrative content and targeted outcomes can meaningfully 
support environmental ed

title: From Sound-Colour Association to Sensory-Affective Worlds:  A Qualitative Case Study of Chromaesthesia in Embodied Music Listening
description: Synesthesia has typically been studied through temporal consistency in inducer--concurrent pairings, privileging stable one-to-one mappings between graphemes/sounds and colours. This qualitative case study examines chromaesthesia (sound-colour synesthesia) as a multisensory, affective, and embodied experience that unfolds during music listening. A semi-structured interview was conducted with an adult with chromaesthesia while listening to Debussy's Clair de lune; the interviewer also had chromaesthesia, and her self-reports during the dialogue were included reflexively in the analysis. The transcript was analyzed using Steps for Coding and Theorization (SCAT). The analysis showed that music-induced concurrents were not limited to colours or shapes, but involved movement, space, temperature, smell, taste, bodily sensation, and affect. These sensory-affective images were organized as coherent motifs and emerged as an integrated sensory world in which the body could be felt as located or oriented. This world was not a reproduction of real scenes; real-world terms served as resources for articulating an idealized sensory world. These findings suggest that chromaesthesia cannot be reduced to sound-colour association, but may render bodily, affective, and abstract musical structures as concrete sensory--affective worlds shaped by memory, learning, and dialogue.

title: Successful Modal Reasoning Depends On WHAT Went WHERE
description: Modal reasoning requires quantifying over possibilities (e.g., categorizing events as necessary, possible, and impossible). This suite of abilities matures during the preschool years, but toddlers perform better in some modal reasoning tasks than others. We propose that these mixed findings reflect a cognitive distinction: toddlers perform worse when reasoning about ambiguous locations of objects (WHERE) than when reasoning about ambiguous kinds of objects (WHAT). In Experiments 1 and 2, we directly compared these forms of ambiguity using matched tasks. Consistent with the hypothesis, toddlers performed substantially better when reasoning about ambiguous kinds than ambiguous locations. Experiment 3 revealed a similar asymmetry in language comprehension, with preschool children showing better comprehension of modal terms such as “can” and “have to” in a kind-based task than in a location task. Thus, modal reasoning emerges earlier than previously suggested, and diversity in results reflects the contributions of distinct cognitive systems.

title: Iatrogenic Harm, Ethics, and Epistemic Justice: A response to Swan et al. (2026)
description: Swan et al. [1] highlight challenges in multidisciplinary care for borderline personality disorder (BPD), including fragmentation and relational strain. This response argues that their analysis is limited by selective engagement with evidence, exclusion of lived experience, and insufficient critique of the diagnostic construct. Evidence indicates that commonly endorsed treatments produce harm, while lived experience research highlights epistemic injustice and identity-related harm. Furthermore, harms associated with BPD may be inherent to the construct itself, not solely consequences of stigma or poor care. These issues have persisted for decades, suggesting structural rather than incidental problems requiring critical re-evaluation of the diagnostic construct.

title: The Moralization of Artificial Intelligence
description: Resistance to artificial intelligence (AI) is widespread and persists even when AI is shown to be instrumentally advantageous. What explains this persistent aversion? Across four studies, we investigate whether moral reactions to AI—beliefs rooted in deeply held notions of right and wrong—explain resistance beyond pragmatic concerns. In Study 1, we analyze moral language in AI-related news headlines from a major US media corpus (COCA, 2018–2024). AI was moralized at levels comparable to GMOs and vaccines, technologies whose moral opposition has received considerable attention. In Studies 2a, 2b, and 3, representative samples of Americans reported attitudes toward several AI applications. Although few participants opposed AI outright (6–44%), most opponents indicated consequence insensitivity, quantity insensitivity, and universalism, suggesting moral motives for opposing AI. Structural equation models revealed that AI moralization was best captured by a single latent factor, indicating a generalized moral sentiment rather than domain-specific risk–benefit appraisals. Qualitative analyses further showed that moralizers typically invoked pragmatic language to justify their opposition. In Study 4, participants from Studies 2b and 3 were re-recruited 75 and 573 days later to complete a behavioral task. Earlier moralization scores predicted greater reluctance to use AI even when instrumentally beneficial—a one standard deviation increase in moralization corresponded to a 42% decrease in AI usage. Together, these findings demonstrate that AI resistance is partly moral in nature, suggesting that reaping the benefits of AI may require addressing moral concerns rather than relying solely on pragmatic arguments.

title: Bayesian Networks for Benchmark Validity in Score Reporting: An ePIRLS Demonstration
description: Large-scale assessments often report achievement through ordered benchmark categories. In PIRLS and ePIRLS, benchmark cut points are derived from the achievement scale and interpreted through scale anchoring. This paper proposes a supplementary Bayesian network (BN) framework for examining whether reported benchmark classifications are supported by local item-response evidence. The framework is not intended to replace item response theory scaling, scale anchoring, or official benchmark procedures. Instead, it treats the benchmark category as an observed reporting classification and evaluates four forms of evidence derived from BN conditional and posterior probabilities: ordering, adjacent-level separation, subgroup transportability, and posterior support for assigned benchmark classifications. Using an ePIRLS 2016 Canadian reading-comprehension subtest with 3,006 students and 17 binary-scored items, the demonstration shows that item-response probabilities were broadly ordered across five benchmark levels, but that evidence varied by item, item type, process of comprehension, benchmark boundary, and language version. Retrieval and Evaluation items showed perfect mean ordering, constructed-response items showed stronger ordering and adjacent separation than multiple-choice items, Integration items showed the smallest average English-French gaps, and posterior support was strongest for middle benchmark levels and weaker at the extremes. The results illustrate how BNs can make benchmark evidence inspectable at the item, item-type, process-of-comprehension, boundary, and subgroup levels. The proposed framework is best understood as a diagnostic validity tool for benchmark interpretation and as a basis for more transparent score-reporting evidence.

title: Disrupting the Mad Genius Myth: Emotional Instability Undermines Creative Self- Beliefs Through Lower Subjective Well-Being in Professional Artists
description: The relationship between emotional instability and creativity in professional artists has long been debated and is often framed through the “mad genius” narrative. Although emotional instability has been associated with creativity, it has also been linked to lower life satisfaction and greater psychological distress, suggesting that it may simultaneously support and undermine creativity-related self-perceptions. This study examined whether life satisfaction and psychological distress mediate the relationship between emotional instability and creative self-beliefs among professional performing artists. A sample of 201 professional performing artists completed the Satisfaction With Life Scale (SWLS), questions from the Generalized Anxiety Disorder Scale (anxiety) and the Patient Health Questionnaire (depression) to measure psychological distress, the Temperament Evaluation of Memphis, Pisa, Paris, and San Diego (TEMPS-A, for emotional instability), and a validated measure of creative self-beliefs. Confirmatory factor analyses and structural equation modelling were conducted. Results indicated that emotional instability positively predicted psychological distress and negatively predicted life satisfaction. Life satisfaction positively predicted creative self-beliefs, whereas psychological distress was not significantly associated with creative self-beliefs. The association between emotional instability and creative self-beliefs was fully mediated by life satisfaction. These findings challenge the “mad genius” narrative by suggesting that life satisfaction is the principal mechanism linking emotional instability to creative self-beliefs.

title: Does Teacher Praise Make Children Feel Less Smart? Two Preregistered Virtual Reality Experiments
description: Does teacher praise make children feel less smart? When two students perform equally, teachers might praise the student they believe worked harder, implicitly conveying to that student that they have lower ability. We tested this hypothesis through two preregistered experiments in a novel Virtual Reality classroom with children aged 7-13 (Study 1: N = 212, Study 2: N = 225). After the child and a virtual classmate performed equally on a task, the teacher praised the child, the classmate, both, or neither. Contrary to hypotheses, there was no evidence that praise made children feel less smart, think that the teacher believed they were less smart, or experience elevated physiological arousal (heart rate, heart rate variability, blushing, skin conductance). Study 2 suggests that children instead viewed praise as a sign of being liked by the teacher. Our studies offer robust evidence that teacher praise may not make children feel less smart.

title: Motives of social media use are differentially associated with mental health outcomes in adolescents
description:
Background: Social media use is ubiquitous among adolescents, yet its relationship with mental health may depend on why it is used. This study distinguishes between avoidant-escapist and social-recreational motives for social media use and examines their associations with mental health, wellbeing, and resilience in a large cohort of UK schoolchildren.
Methods: Cross-sectional data were drawn from the BrainWaves study (N = 6820, Mage = 16.72). Social media motives were assessed using 10 items and derived using exploratory factor analysis (EFA) into two latent factors: avoidant-escapist (boredom, addiction, distraction, procrastination) and social-recreational (socialising, communication, entertainment, observation) use. Confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) was used to estimate factor scores, which were examined in linear regression models. Structural equation modelling (SEM) was then applied to estimate associations with anxiety, depression, wellbeing, and resilience, adjusting for gender and deprivation.
Results: In linear regression analyses, avoidant-escapist social media use was associated with higher anxiety and depressive symptoms, whereas social-recreational use was associated with lower levels of both outcomes. No interaction between gender and social media motives was observed. The SEM was a good fit to the data and showed that avoidant-escapist use was associated with higher anxiety and depressive symptoms, and lower wellbeing and resilience. In contrast, social-recreational use was associated with lower anxiety and depressive symptoms, and higher wellbeing and resilience. 
Conclusions: The associations between social media use and adolescent mental health differ by underlying motives. Avoidant-escapist use is linked to poorer outcomes, whereas social-recreational use is associated with more favourable outcomes. Focusing on why adolescents engage with social media, rather than overall use alone, is necessary for understanding risk and informing interventions.

title: A Conversation Guide to Support Color-Conscious Racial Socialization among White Parent-Child Dyads
description: Family discussions may be an important context for shaping White children’s developing racial attitudes, yet the majority of White parents in the U.S. report that they either de-emphasize or avoid discussions of race and racism with their White children. The current study presents a qualitative analysis of racial messages communicated during a guided discussion task designed to scaffold color-conscious conversations about vignettes depicting interpersonal racism. Participants, recruited from a Midwestern U.S. city between 2018 and 2020, included 87 self-identified White parents (91.5% women, 8.5% men; Mage = 42.57 years, SD = 5.14) and their parent-identified White children (ages 8–12; 53% girls, 47% boys; Mage = 8.95 years, SD = 1.16). Most parents were highly educated, middle-class or upper-middle-class, married, and liberal or liberal-leaning. Findings revealed that many parents and children used racial language and endorsed color-conscious messages, such as acknowledging that racial prejudice had occurred in the vignettes. However, some dyads redirected the conversation away from race or made external attributions for racist behavior rather than attributing responsibility to White perpetrators. Together, these findings suggest that structured scaffolding may support more explicit conversations about racism in White families while also highlighting variability in how parents and children interpret and discuss racist behavior.

title: What is it to be aware? A Pragmatic Approach to Comparing Animal Awareness
description: Efforts to understand animal abilities face longstanding conceptual and methodological challenges, especially regarding cognition and consciousness. Awareness has largely suffered a similar fate, having been subsumed into these discussions rather than examined on its own merit. This paper asks what it means to be aware. The proposal is to understand it as an organism’s abilities to selectively process, store, and use information in the service of goal-directed action. A pragmatic approach to awareness for comparative research is developed and briefly illustrated through an example of spatial awareness in desert ants.

title: No evidence for predicting from conflict: A reverse cueing study reveals the limits of congruency-stimulus learning
description: The interplay between cognitive control, memory, and learning is as relevant as it is elusive. Despite broad interest in the notion that people learn to adjust control in response to cues, consensus on control learning is lacking. Previous research struggled to find evidence for cross-trial control learning when different levels of control were cued by stimulus features of the previous trial. We examined whether these inconsistencies arise from a general inability to prepare for control, or from an inability to encode control information within cross-trial associations. To test this, we turned around the cue-control paradigm by using a Stroop task where congruency levels (i.e., control demands) predicted target colors (i.e., stimulus features). Four independent experiments (n = 50; 125; 50; 56) were conducted. We found that people struggle to learn to benefit from congruency-color associations, with no clear evidence for faster reaction times on trials preceded by predictive congruency levels. Post-hoc analyses suggest that participants may have integrated individual congruency-color sequences into predictor-outcome episodes and retrieved these episodes when encountering a given congruency value, only facilitating performance when the same congruency-color sequence was repeated. Overall, our findings suggest that people are largely unable to use control levels as cues to predict task-relevant features across trials, indicating that task-generated conflict may not function effectively as a cue. However, we also offer a novel interpretative framework for researchers interested in investigating episodic retrieval in control-learning paradigms.

title: The relationship between social media use and social isolation in young adults: a systematic review
description: Social isolation has become a growing public health concern, with increasing attention to the potential role of social media in shaping social connection and disconnection. This systematic review synthesises 21 empirical studies published between 2000 and 2024 that examined associations between social media use and social isolation among young adults. Following the PRISMA guidelines, studies were selected from five databases: PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, EBSCOhost, and Google Scholar. Thematic analysis identified three major categories: (1) motivations and patterns of social media use, (2) Effects of Text-based and Visual Communication Channels, and (3) No Association Between Social Media and Social Isolation. While 15 studies reported a positive association between certain patterns of social media use and increased feelings of isolation, four identified potential benefits, and two found no significant relationships. Specifically, excessive or passive use without interaction was more commonly linked to negative outcomes, whereas purposeful and interactive use appeared to support social connection. Differences in platform specifics (e.g., text-based vs. image-based) and contextual variables such as the COVID-19 pandemic contributed to the variability of results. Most studies adopted cross-sectional designs and applied varied measurement tools, which may have influenced the consistency and comparability of results.

title: Beyond Individual Resilience: Institutional Stressors, Burnout, and Coping among Baptist Pastors in Urban Ghana
description:
Background: Baptist pastors in Ghana face intense urban pressures, yet empirical studies on their occupational wellbeing are scarce. This research investigates burnout and institutional conflict, utilizing a novel socio ecological framework to uniquely link macro environmental pressures with denominational policy.
Methods: A cross sectional survey instrument was administered to 200 ordained GBC pastors in Kumasi. Using Python, descriptive statistics, Pearson and Spearman correlations, Cronbach alpha reliability, Kruskal Wallis, and chi square analyses were computed alongside qualitative content analysis. A novel four level conceptual framework mapped distal context, proximal stressors, and coping strategies.
Results: Church conflict was highest rated (M = 3.51, SD = 1.00; 71.5% agreement), followed by training gaps (64.5%) and work life imbalance (63.5%). Qualitative findings highlighted financial pressure, burnout, and family disruption. Mid career pastors (11-20 years) exhibited highest burnout, which did not differ significantly by location. Sabbaticals (55.5%), training (53.5%), prayer and fasting (52.0%), peer support (50.5%), and professional counselling (44.5%) were common coping strategies.
Conclusions: The novel framework reveals that pastoral distress is a systemic crisis driven by institutional deficits rather than individual vulnerability. Distal urban pressures interact with proximal stressors to generate distributed distress, which is only partially moderated by coping resources. By conceptualizing these dynamic, nested connections, the framework provides a comprehensive roadmap for GBC policy interventions, demonstrating that the denomination must establish funded mental health systems, reform mandatory transfer policies, and implement structured continuing education pathways to proactively address early career vulnerability and ensure long term ministerial health across sub Saharan Africa.

title: The Experimental Study of Habitual Behavior in Humans: A Review of the Validity of Current Protocols
description: Although habits are widely recognized as playing a key role across psychological science, current laboratory methods may limit our understanding of these behaviors. Within the dual‑system framework, habits are defined as context-triggered, outcome‑insensitive responses that emerge gradually with repeated instrumental training. Many human experimental paradigms have been developed in an attempt to test this characterization of habits. However, in most cases, they have not provided clear evidence of habit formation, suggesting a gap between habit theory and existing methodologies. In the present study, we systematically review evidence on the construct validity of fourteen paradigms in which the amount of training was manipulated. We also reanalyze publicly available datasets from studies using these paradigms to assess the psychometric reliability of their main measures, thereby extending the available validity evidence. Paradigms that most closely mirror classical approaches derived from habit theory have consistently failed to induce habits, whereas more recent approaches have revealed training effects. However, these novel paradigms often rely on broader operationalizations that substantially diverge from traditional definitions of habit. Among the paradigms reviewed, the forced‑response task stands out as capable of inducing habitual behavior while providing a narrowly operationalized measure with acceptable reliability. Finally, we argue that strengthening the credibility of the field will require greater attention to the psychometric properties of habit measures, including precise operationalization, reliability, and systematic validity testing.

title: Situational and longitudinal associations between motivational beliefs, anxiety, and learning during retrieval practice
description: Motivational and emotional processes are presumed to play a key role in shaping who engages in retrieval practice. Furthermore, students' success or struggle with retrieval practice may shape their subsequent motivations and emotions, yielding “feedback loops” in which these processes are mutually linked. Building upon situated expectancy-value theory and control-value theory, the present study examined a) concurrent intraindividual associations between control and value beliefs, anxiety, and engagement and achievement during retrieval practice, b) their reciprocal intraindividual associations over time, and c) whether students' aggregated motivational and emotional experiences predicted their end-of-term achievement and anxiety. In addition to an begin- and end-of-term questionnaire, students (N=636) participated and reported their motivational experiences weekly during retrieval practice sessions across a semester. Dynamic structural equation models revealed that control, intrinsic value, and utility value were negatively related to anxiety, while cost was positively related to students' anxiety during retrieval practice. Anxiety was negatively associated with engagement and achievement. Additionally, reciprocal within-person associations indicative of feedback loops emerged, with engagement and partly achievement relating positively to subsequent control and value. Students' aggregated achievement during retrieval practice positively predicted their end-of-semester achievement, whereas trait- and aggregated state motivational and emotional experiences showed no incremental predictive effects. However, higher aggregated state anxiety was associated with higher end-of-semester test anxiety. Overall, these findings suggest that retrieval practice exercises can contribute to self-reinforcing motivational-emotional cycles across the semester, pointing to a pathway through which momentary experiences during retrieval practice may accumulate into end-of-term differences

title: A Dialectical Model of Self-Love: Worth, Compassion, and Embodied Self-Engagement
description: Although the concept of self-love has gained cultural and clinical prominence, it remains theoretically diffuse and frequently conflated with self-esteem, narcissism, or self-compassion. This article proposes a dialectically structured framework that conceptualizes self-love as a dynamic mode of self-relation rather than a static trait or evaluative attitude. The model identifies three interdependent dimensions: (1) inherent worth, defined as the recognition and protection of non-contingent dignity and value; (2) self-compassion, conceptualized as a regulatory process balancing soothing and corrective motivation in response to distress; and (3) embodied self-engagement, defined as the bodily capacity to remain present with activation, pleasure, effort, and intensity without abandoning contact with oneself. Each dimension contains an internal tension between receptive and agentic functions, allowing self-relation to remain flexible across contexts of success, failure, and growth. By specifying the integration of evaluative, compassionate, and embodied processes, the framework offers a conceptual account of self-love as a flexible mode of self-relation across conditions of comfort, adversity, activation, and change. The article outlines conceptual distinctions from related constructs and proposes a programmatic agenda for empirical validation.

title: Good Kitty, Bad Bank? Rescoring Miscalibrated CATs Improves Accuracy
description: Computerized adaptive tests (CAT) depend on accurately calibrated item banks, but in practice, the item parameters governing deployment of the item banks are often based on small pilot samples, transported across populations, or assigned placeholder values pending proper calibration. We decompose the impact of miscalibration on subsequent ability estimates into two components: item selection error and scoring error. While selection error is not recoverable, rescoring using better calibrations, and without any additional testing burden, can potentially provide a post-hoc fix to scoring errors.  In a simulation study, we find that rescoring substantially reduces root mean squared error (RMSE), with scoring error accounting for 86 to 96% of miscalibration-attributable error. In Study 2, we apply this framework to data from 2,657 children (ages 5 to 12) assessed across three pilot sites in the LEVANTE project. Using identical scoring methods with old versus new item parameters, we found that rescoring shifted scores substantially and reordered children's relative standing; external validation confirms the rescored estimates are better, not just different. Low-ability and younger children are disproportionately affected by rescoring, underscoring the equity implications. These results highlight the utility of rescoring for any CAT using early-stage, transported, or AI-generated item parameters, and how rescoring can enable rapid deployment of assessments to new populations.

title: Emotion Regulation Partially Mediates the Relation Between Stressful Life Event Exposure and Adolescent Psychopathology
description: Stressful life event exposure (SLEE) is robustly linked with adolescent psychopathology, and prior work suggests emotion regulation (ER) may mediate this relation. However, research incorporating experiences of gender diverse (GD) adolescents has been lacking, despite elevated rates of SLEE and psychopathology in GD individuals. This study examined gender and sex differences in relations between SLEE, ER, and psychopathology in the longitudinal Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study. One thousand five hundred eighty-one cisgender (cis) boys, 1439 cis girls, and 169 GD adolescents reported SLEE via the Life Events Scale in early adolescence (M±SD: 11.999±0.648 years), ER difficulties via the Difficulties in Emotion Regulation Scale-Parent Report one year later (M±SD: 12.931±0.644 years), and internalizing and externalizing psychopathology symptoms via the Brief Problem Monitor-Youth Report an additional year later (M±SD: 14.129±0.681 years). Mediation and moderated mediation analyses were conducted using conditional process modeling. ER difficulties partially mediated relations between SLEE and psychopathology symptoms. Gender moderated relations between SLEE and internalizing symptoms, but not externalizing symptoms, such that direct relations between SLEE and internalizing symptoms were stronger for GD youth and cis girls compared to cis boys.  Moderated mediation models with gender as the moderator explained more variance in internalizing symptoms compared to models with sex as the moderator, while models with gender and sex explained similar amounts of variance in externalizing symptoms. Findings highlighted: (1) ER difficulties as a partial mediator of relations between SLEE and psychopathology, and (2) differences in direct relations between SLEE and internalizing symptoms based on gender.

title: Defining Wellness: Conceptions of Ideal Mental Health in Ancient Yogic Texts and Contemporary Indian Views
description:
The prevailing modern operationalisations of positive mental health have been criticised for their inherent focus on sense-based, egotistical happiness. Addressing this concern, many contemporary mental health professionals have turned to indigenous ideas and classical philosophical texts to gain insights into optimal well-being. With the same aim, a cross-sectional, mixed-methods exploratory research was designed to uncover the meanings of ideal mental health among 240 urban adults (Male =136, Female = 104; mean age, 38.17 years) from North India, along with exploring themes of ideal mental health in selected classical texts from Indian psychology, i.e., The Bhagavad Gita (700 verses) and Patanjali’s Yogasutras (196 verses). Their content analysis revealed five broad themes: Sthitaprajñā (Steady wisdom), Anasakti (Non-attachment), Svadharma (Personal duty),  Shraddha (Faith), Ishwar Pranidhana (Surrender to the Divine/God). From the thematic analysis of subjective meanings, two major themes emerged: Describing ideal mental state as a positive mental state and Dismissive attitude towards ideal mental state. A notable similarity was found between the traditional, non-egotistical understanding of mental health and contemporary community aspirations in India. However, there were certain critical differences in opinions regarding the attainability of such goals. This research provides important contextual evidence that can help expand the framework of well-being.
Keywords: Ideal mental health, Yogic scriptures, well-being, Indian psychology

title: Adolescents value learning about a newly acquainted peer in a face-to-face interaction
description: Adolescence is a developmental period characterized by heightened importance of peers. Adolescents actively seek out opportunities to learn about peers, while discriminating between different peers in the learning process. Previous work has predominantly focused on how youth value learning about close friends, popular kids, or majority opinions, and has not yet investigated how adolescents may value learning about other sources of peer information, such as a peer they have just met. Here, we present findings from a novel behavioral task in which adolescents 11-15 years old had the opportunity to earn money as they made choices to learn information about a newly acquainted peer interaction partner (‘interaction peer’), the most common response of other adolescents their age (‘majority peer’), or trivia facts. Adolescents valued learning about the interaction peer over the majority peer and trivia facts, giving up nearly a penny for each opportunity to learn about the interaction peer. They also valued learning about the majority peer over trivia. Age and gender significantly interacted to predict heterogeneity in youth’s choices: with increasing age, male adolescents were increasingly motivated to learn about the majority peer, while female adolescents were decreasingly motivated to learn about the majority peer. Together, these results highlight gender differences in how peer information is valued across adolescent development. Characterizing how youth value learning about peers informs understanding of the way peers impact adolescents’ social worlds through relationship development and social influence.

title: Distinct Neural Representations across Discrete and Continuous Non-symbolic Ratios
description: Relative magnitudes, such as ratios and proportions, are crucial to everyday life. According to the ratio processing system (RPS) theory, ratios across different formats share a common neural code. Prior neuroimaging studies have shown that ratios across different visual formats are processed by overlapping brain areas, thus providing support for this hypothesis. However, overlapping activation found from univariate analyses does not necessarily imply common representations. The aim of this study was to probe the key prediction of the RPS theory by investigating the neural representation of ratios depicted in discrete and continuous magnitudes using multivariate fMRI analyses. Thirty participants completed a delayed ratio comparison task on discrete (sets of dots) and continuous (line lengths) magnitudes while in the MRI scanner. Using representational similarity analysis (RSA), we examined the similarity between ratio representations across high-level variations, such as magnitude type (length and numerosity), and low-level variations, such as variations in line orientation and dot size, throughout the brain, notably in parietal areas. Results did not support a common ratio representation across discrete and continuous magnitudes. Instead, ratios in numerosity and length seemed to be encoded in qualitatively distinct ways. Altogether, results suggest that ratios are not represented in a format-independent way in the brain, thus challenging the RPS theory.

title: Beyond the Western Canon: Broadening the Foundations of Psychological Science
description: Modern psychology has attended closely to the limits of WEIRD samples. At the same time, the field has paid far less attention to the foundational narrative which preceded and contributed to a WEIRD sampling bias. This paper connects skews sampling to a WEIRD philosophy of mind, expressed through two interconnected canons: an institutional canon that centers Euro-American laboratory psychology and a philosophical canon that incorrectly represents questions of mind as emerging primarily from a Western intellectual lineage. Drawing on transregional histories of psychological science and philosophies of mind, the paper formulates a broader institutional and philosophical canon and discusses the contributions of scholars, traditions, and intellectual lineages often left outside psychology’s standard narrative. The aim of this paper is to broaden the historical and conceptual foundations of psychological science and thus expand areas of inquiry and explanatory frameworks available to the field.

title: Rated E for Emotional: Children's Understanding of Death, Conversations About Death, and Parental Predictors
description: Understanding death involves integrating biological, spiritual, and affective concepts, which are shaped by watching media and interacting with parents. However, parents sometimes shield children from information about death because they believe the children are too young to understand it. We examined the alignment between children’s actual understanding of death and their parents’ predictions of their understanding. We also had dyads watch and discuss a short animated film depicting death to observe their conversations about death. We recruited 68 4- to 6-year-olds (31M, 36F, 1NB; 56% White) and their parents from the United States from April 2024 to May 2025. We found that children’s biological understanding increases with age, whereas spiritual and affective understanding remained stable across this age period. Parents tended to overestimate their children’s understanding of several biological and affective aspects of death, suggesting that parents’ shielding beliefs are not related to children’s actual understanding of death. Although most families mentioned death, their conversations were brief, showing that death conversations are more common and less in-depth than prior research suggests. Parents had an active role in the conversation and focused predominantly on affective aspects of death. These findings highlight that promoting in-depth conversations about death might require supporting parents.

title: Optimizing Care for Older Transgender and Non-Binary Adults: A Co-created Agenda for Future Research
description:
Background
Despite a growing population of older transgender and non-binary (TNB) adults, evidence-based guidance for their care remains limited. There is a pressing need for a comprehensive research agenda developed in collaboration with, rather than solely about, this population.
Aim
This study aimed to co-create key areas and priorities for future research to improve quality of care for older TNB adults.
Methods
A four-day workshop was held with a group of 19 TNB individuals, clinicians, and academic researchers, representing diverse lived experiences, ages, occupations, and cultural backgrounds. A series of lived experience and scientific presentations were given and co-creation sessions were held to collaboratively explore the study’s aim. Concept mapping and design thinking principles were employed to generate and thematically organize insights during co-creation sessions. Data transcripts were then further analyzed using template analysis in consultation with co-creators.
Results
Three overarching themes were constructed. The first theme (reframing research best practice) offers guidance on future research conduct, emphasizing the importance of adopting participatory approaches, inclusivity, and the expansion of methodological perspectives to better capture complexity. The second theme (addressing knowledge gaps) highlights gaps in our understanding of gender-affirming medical care in older age and biopsychosocial influences on health. The third theme (practice-based research and knowledge mobilization) focuses on support for known challenges such as limited social support, best practice in elderly care, recognition and navigation of systemic power structures, and effective translation and dissemination of knowledge.
Discussion
This co-created agenda is intended to catalyze more responsive, inclusive, and equitable research and practice, ensuring that the voices and needs of older TNB adults remain central to efforts aimed at promoting healthy aging and quali

title: A selection of environmental sounds for behavioural and neuroimaging research: Introducing the EnviSounds dataset
description: With growing interest in ecologically valid stimuli and the proliferation of recognition and classification algorithms, environmental sounds are increasingly a topic of interest and study. However, there is a lack of consensus as to which sound categories should be selected, and which exemplars should represent these categories. Indeed, many existing datasets include only one exemplar per sound class. This is not characteristic of the actual acoustic environment and can lead to brittle and unrepresentative computational solutions and experimental results. Importantly, the existing literature provides relatively little information about how human listeners perceive the recognizability, similarity and representativeness of acoustically and perceptually varying sounds. Here, we introduce the Environmental Sounds (EnviSounds) dataset. It provides data from over 1000 human listeners performing different tasks (recognition, similarity judgement, goodness of fit) on 53 commonly encountered environmental sound categories of human, natural and man-made sounds, each represented by 10 different exemplars. We provide behavioural indices of within-class similarity and goodness of exemplar for all samples. Furthermore, we include normative data for recognition and identification latency, accuracy, and imageability, enabling researchers to select items for experiments based on pre-defined criteria across these dimensions. With this dataset, environmental sounds can be considered at various levels of complexity: sounds produced by the same sources varying in their acoustics (within-class acoustic variability) and acoustically similar sounds produced by different sources (between-category confusion). The dataset can be used for specifying training sets with individual sound sources, defining the categorical boundaries, or providing additional variables to building prediction models.

title: Environmental Dynamics and Exam Stress among Nigerian  Adolescents: The Mitigating Role of Regional Community Support Structures
description:
This study investigates the structural relationship between external environmental 
stressors, local community support networks, and examination-induced anxiety among 
secondary school seniors preparing for high-stakes standardized assessments in Nigeria. 
Using a descriptive quantitative survey layout framework, data was collected from a 
cross-sectional sample of N=95 Senior Secondary School 3 (SS3) students at Rochas 
Foundation College (Owerri, Imo State). Structural metrics focused on evaluating the 
mitigating capacity of multi-tier support structures, specifically comparing localized 
family communication channels and informal peer group interaction dynamics against 
standardized stress markers. Quantitative analysis revealed that peer support 
environments served as the primary self-reported buffer against exam panic, yielding a
dominant mean structural preference ranking of 1.38, followed closely by familial 
support networks at 1.69. Crucially, candidates lacking robust peer group integration 
exhibited extreme examination anxiety indices averaging 18.63 out of a 20-point max 
scale, whereas students with high peer-tier positioning dropped significantly to a mean 
stress index of 15.10, representing an empirical 18.91% buffer in psychological stress 
resilience. Lived-experience frameworks were integrated utilizing existential coping
metrics to evaluate individual cognitive adaptation under pressure. The findings suggest 
that structural implementation of peer-led learning circles within secondary academic 
institutions offers a low-cost, high-impact behavioral intervention to optimize student 
mental health during high-pressure educational transitions.

title: Behavioral Emotion Regulation in Internalizing Disorders: A Transdiagnostic Psychometric Evaluation of the German Behavioral Emotion Regulation Questionnaire (BERQ)
description:
Background
