Behavioral emotion regulation (ER) is conceptually distinct from cognitive ER, yet dedicated instruments to assess behavioral strategies are limited and rarely validated in clinical samples. Both ER domains relate to of the psychopathology of internalizing disorders, with potentially different contributions across diagnoses. 

Aims
This study evaluates the psychometric properties of the German version of the Behavioral Emotion Regulation Questionnaire (BERQ), including its factorial structure, reliability, construct validity, and measurement invariance across gender and three diagnostic groups: unipolar depression, anxiety disorders, and obsessive-compulsive disorder.

Methods
Baseline data from N = 462 outpatients with internalizing disorders prior to cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) were analyzed. Confirmatory factor analyses with subsample cross-validation, as well as measurement invariance testing and correlational and regression analyses, were conducted to evaluate the BERQ and its associations with clinical measures and other ER measures.

Results
The five-factor structure of the BERQ was supported, with good internal consistency and measurement invariance across gender and diagnostic groups. Several behavioral strategies were significantly associated with depressive symptoms and global symptom severity, with withdrawal showing the most pronounced effects. Behavioral ER explained additional variance in symptom severity beyond cognitive ER strategies. Latent mean differences indicated clinically relevant differences across diagnostic groups. 

Conclusions
The findings support the German BERQ as a reliable and valid instrument for assessing behavioral ER in clinical populations and highlight the relevance of behavioral strategies for understanding the psychopathology of internalizing disorders. Improved measurement of behavioral ER may therefore contribute to advances in targeted interventions and clinical research.

title: Metacontingency Analysis of Practices Associated to Mental Health
description:
This article proposes an analysis of mental health and psychotherapy as a result of cultural practices, based on contextual behavioral science, which combines behavioral analysis and cultural analysis. Similarly, it proposes complementing the analysis of public policy and other regulatory instruments with analytical tools from this scientific perspective, such as metacontingencies and macrocontingencies, which allow us to understand a policy or any regulatory instrument as a metacontingency system capable of constructing cultural practices related to mental health and facilitate the analysis of molar and molecular factors in psychotherapy. Reference is made to the case of Colombia as a country with particular conditions that could be addressed with an integrated model. Finally, methodological challenges and implications are addressed.
Keywords: metacontingencies; macrocontingencies; cultural practices; psychotherapy; public policy and mental health.

title: Social media and smartphone use are associated with blunted striatal reward response in early adolescence
description: Adolescents spend unprecedented time on smartphones, raising concerns that screen time, and social media use in particular, may negatively impact developing reward circuitry in the brain—the very system critical for motivation and flexible learning. We tested whether social media and overall smartphone use are associated with altered risk-taking, neural responsivity, and mental health outcomes in early adolescence. Twenty-nine participants (ages 13-15) completed a reinforcement learning gambling task while undergoing fMRI. We fit a computational model to estimate trial-wise reward prediction errors (RPEs) during a gambling task and quantified striatal RPE sensitivity, a canonical neural signature of dopaminergic reward learning. We also measured time spent on social media applications and total daily smartphone use. Adolescents averaged nearly 6 hours of screen time per day and exhibited strong preferences for the social media apps TikTok and Snapchat. Greater social media use predicted increased gambling behavior, indicating increased reward-seeking behavior. Increased screen time and social media use were associated with blunted striatal activity, suggesting a reduced neural responsiveness to rewards. App-specific analyses indicate that these diminished striatal responses were largely driven by TikTok use. Finally, smartphone use was associated with greater anxiety, depression, and intolerance of uncertainty, which were also related to reduced striatal sensitivity. These findings provide evidence consistent with an emerging maladaptive profile that links technology exposure, mental health, and reward circuit function.

title: Object perception encodes mutually exclusive possibilities
description: Human adults represent and reason about possibilities: multiple, mutually exclusive, non-actual ways the world could be. It is debated whether this is a late-developing, human-specific capacity and whether it requires natural language. We propose that instead of a unitary high-level capacity, multiple cognitive capacities might independently represent possibilities in different ways and with different properties. Our case study is object perception, a capacity shared with infants and non-human animals. Using methods that tap specifically into visual processes, across four experiments (N = 160), we found possibility representations in vision tasks that do not involve high-level reasoning or language. In Experiments 1 and 2, we found evidence for the visual encoding of possible object identities: When there were two possible ways that features might map onto visual objects, both possible mappings were primed. In Experiment 3, we found that visual feature-binding is a necessary precondition for such priming, ruling out low-level associative and high-level reasoning-based alternatives. Finally, in Experiment 4, we discovered that the visual system cannot encode one visual object possibly being at two possible locations. This pattern helps to explain a host of previous findings from the comparative and developmental literature and suggests that the unit of analysis for possibility representations should be the cognitive capacity rather than the agent.

title: Common Humanity and Resilience: A Scoping Review
description:
Objectives: Social support and self-compassion are well-established predictors of resilience across diverse populations and contexts. While the associations between resilience and both social support and self-compassion are well documented in the literature, common humanity—a subcomponent of self-compassion related to social support that involves recognizing the universality of painful experiences—has received comparatively little attention in resilience research. Accordingly, a scoping review was conducted to map the empirical literature on common humanity and resilience, synthesize their associations, and examine definitions and conceptualizations of both constructs.
Methods: To identify studies, a search strategy was developed and executed across seven databases. The titles and abstracts as well as the full texts of emerging publications were independently screened by three reviewers. Data from 40 studies that met the inclusion criteria by consensus were extracted and summarized.
Results: Among the 4,353 references identified, findings from 40 included studies indicate a consistent positive relationship between common humanity and resilience, with higher common humanity associated with more effective coping, adaptation, and recovery from adversity. Regardless of the definitions and conceptualizations of both common humanity and resilience—as well as differences in geographic location, research type, study population, sample size, or form of adversity under investigation—common humanity consistently evidenced a robust association with resilience. Nevertheless, this relationship varied depending on the constructs examined, the form of adversity studied, the underlying mechanisms, and the conceptualizations of common humanity. These results elucidate the association between common humanity and resilience while identifying the factors that shape this relationship.

title: Aesthetic value is behaviorally and neurally dissociable from reinforcement value
description: Is aesthetic value represented separately from other value signals? “Common Neural Currency” accounts of value hold that all forms of value are encoded similarly within the Brain Valuation System (BVS). Yet while reinforcement value arises from conditioning with tangible rewards (e.g. food, money) that produce approach or avoidance (incentive salience), theoretical accounts of aesthetic value suggest that it results from perceptual and conceptual sense-making (“pleasure from understanding”), and imaging evidence suggests that aesthetic value is encoded in fine-grain activity patterns of the Default Mode Network (DMN). We therefore investigated whether aesthetic value is behaviorally and neurally dissociable from reinforcement value. Human observers rated their aesthetic appeal for a set of abstract visual images, which were then associated with differential reinforcement values in a monetary reinforcement paradigm. Aesthetic value did not affect reinforcement, and reinforcement only minimally impacted subsequent aesthetic ratings. In a brain imaging experiment using fMRI, we found distinct neural signatures for reinforcement history and aesthetic value in the BVS and DMN, and common value coding in the ventral medial prefrontal cortex. Unlike reinforcement, aesthetic value was reflected in fine-grain activity patterns of the DMN and in activity of higher-level perceptual regions. Thus, while aesthetic value and reinforcement are not entirely independent, aesthetic value is a psychologically distinct construct that is both behaviorally and neurally dissociable from reinforcement value.

title: Planning paths not taken: False memories for unexecuted actions
description: Action planning involves representing multiple possible actions, including alternatives that are ultimately not taken. While such representations support flexible behaviour, they may also bias memory for one's own actions. Participants (N = 24) performed a goal-directed maze navigation task in which they planned routes with multiple alternatives before executing a chosen path, followed by a recognition memory test. On some trials, an available path was blocked after planning, forcing participants to revise their plan. False memories were higher for paths that were blocked than for unchosen but still-available alternatives, and this effect was strongest when the blocked path was the shortest available route. This pattern suggests that the depth to which a route is incorporated into an action plan determines the strength of its subsequent mnemonic trace. A second experiment (N = 33) confirmed that the effect requires prior plannability and cannot be explained by the visual salience of the block alone. Together, these findings reveal a direct link between action planning and memory distortion for one's own actions.

title: Silent and Underestimated Climate Change Concern Without Behavioural Backlash: Findings From a Representative Dutch Survey on Climate Change Communication
description:
Notwithstanding the scientific evidence and widespread concern about climate change, insufficient action is being taken to mitigate it. The misperceived social norm that others do not care about climate change—conceptualized as pluralistic ignorance—and a lack of interpersonal communication about topics related to climate change are seen as possible inhibitors of climate action and pro-environmental behavior. However, empirical evidence on the relationship between pluralistic ignorance, climate change communication, and pro-environmental behavior is sparse.
We surveyed a representative Dutch sample (N = 926). Most participants talked about climate change-related topics with friends and family less than once per month or “occasionally”. Using one-sample t-tests we found empirical support for pluralistic ignorance, with participants underestimating levels of climate change importance, worry, and felt individual responsibility. Regression analyses showed that hearing others talk about climate change negatively predicted pluralistic ignorance, while talking more often with people who share one’s opinion positively predicted pluralistic ignorance. Contrary to our expectations, participants reporting higher levels of pluralistic ignorance engaged in more pro-environmental behavior. An additional investigation of a small sample of climate change communication experts (N = 56) furthermore demonstrated the existence of pluralistic ignorance in individuals talking frequently about climate change. 
Our findings suggest that most adults in the Netherlands talk about climate change infrequently and that engaging in these conversations is not necessarily linked to a more accurate picture of climate change concern levels. At the same time, pluralistic ignorance did not seem to be linked to the expected problematic collective bystander effect.

title: Effectiveness and uptake of ROOM to grow: Results of a randomized controlled trial
description:
Background
One in four university students face mental health challenges, underscoring the need for effective support systems. Within Erasmus University Rotterdam student wellbeing initiative, we developed a mobile intervention providing universal and targeted preventive support, focusing on emotion regulation to address common issues like depression and anxiety. This study reports the results of a superiority Randomized Controlled Trial testing the intervention impact and uptake.
Methods
Students (N = 202) were randomized to immediate ROOM app access (n = 101) or a 3-month waitlist control (n = 101); 171 (85%) completed the trial. Questionnaires were completed at baseline and weeks 3, 8, and 12, alongside continuous in-app activity logs. Primary outcomes were perceived stress and emotion regulation; secondary outcomes included depressive and anxiety symptoms, resilience, and objective and subjective engagement. Analyses followed an intent-to-treat approach, with exploratory subgroup analyses assessing differences by engagement level.
Results
The intervention showed no statistically significant impact on any outcomes. Subgroup analyses suggested that highly engaged users experienced reduced stress, while moderately engaged users showed improved resilience but elevated depressive symptoms. Engagement was initially high but declined sharply after week 1, stabilizing by week 6. More than half of participants still used the intervention at day 30. Breathing and relaxation exercises were favoured, whereas transfer-elements and self-assessments were used less than expected.
Conclusions
 ROOM showed limited overall impact but yielded benefits for highly engaged users. Future refinement should focus on identifying how much and what type of engagement is needed for the app to effectively support students.

title: Transitions in Teachers’ Technology Utilization: Evidence from a Large-Scale, Longitudinal, and International Panel Study
description: Teachers’ technology utilization varies substantially within and across educational systems, yet its longitudinal dynamics remain poorly understood. Using data from the International Computer and Information Literacy Study (ICILS) 2018-2020 Teacher Panel Study covering Denmark, Finland, and Uruguay, this study examined latent profiles of teachers’ ICT utilization, their stability and change over time, and associations with teacher characteristics. Profiles ranged from minimally engaged to comprehensive integrators, with intermediate profiles reflecting selective or functionally embedded ICT use. Two theoretically important profiles exhibited a paradoxical combination of positive ICT attitudes and low classroom practice, consistent with second-order barriers to technology integration. Profile stability varied cross-nationally, with Finland showing the greatest stability and Uruguay exhibiting a consolidation of profiles between occasions. ICT self-efficacy and collaborative ICT use were the most consistent predictors of lower-engagement profile membership. Our findings highlight cross-national heterogeneity in ICT utilization profiles and a persistent attitude-practice gap across educational systems. Effective professional development should target barriers preventing attitudinally committed teachers from enacting ICT in practice, with collaborative teaching cultures as a key enabling condition.

title: Measurement of American adolescents’ experiences of online harms: A nationally representative survey
description:
Importance: Concerns about the risks adolescents face online are rising, but existing research on online harms typically examines limited outcomes, rarely allows for platform-specific comparison, and lacks practical standardized measurement that would be suitable for public health monitoring.
Objective: We introduce and implement a measurement approach estimating the prevalence of negative experiences among US adolescents online, offline, and by platform.
Design, Setting, and Participants: Cross-sectional, nationally representative, probability-based survey of US adolescents aged 13-17 conducted February-December 2025 through the Understanding America Study panel. Self-reported use of 20 online platforms (e.g. Facebook, Instagram, Snapchat, TikTok, YouTube, Facetime, email etc) was assessed.
Main Outcomes and Measures: Self-reported prevalence of major risks and harms experienced in past 4 weeks, including harassment, sexual solicitation, and exposure to violent or self-harm content, as well as sleep disruption (measured online, offline, and by platform). Survey-weighted logistic regression identified associated factors.
Results: Weighted sample included 482 adolescents (mean age 15 years; 47.1% female; 65.1% White) from 47 US states. Across online and offline contexts, 44.3% witnessed harassment and 29.6% had experienced it directly in the past 4 weeks. Overall prevalence varied by gender and age: girls were more likely than boys to feel worse about themselves due to others' posts, messages, or communications (29.1% vs 15.5%), and older adolescents (ages 15-17) were more likely than younger adolescents (ages 13-14) to have witnessed discrimination against others (48.6% vs 38.5%). Online exposure exceeded offline exposure for numerous harms, including exposure to violent imagery (10.5% vs 1.6%), unwanted sexual images (13.5% vs 2.0%), and content encouraging self-harm (9.6% vs 5.1%). title: A test of the digital Give-a-Number task
description: For over 50 years, the Give-a-Number task has been used as a measure of children’s understanding of number words. Also, the knower level framework that results from the task has also featured prominently in theoretical proposals about children’s number acquisition and the development of number concepts. However, because different labs test children with different objects, trial structures, and numbers, the field lacks a standardized version of the task that can be used as a stable predictor across studies. In this study, we took a step toward standardization by asking whether a digital version of the task could replace the standard version. When individual children were tested with both a physical act-out version and a digital version of Give-a-Number, we found moderate to high concordance between the two versions. However, we also found that children tended to perform more accurately on the physical version, though this difference had little effect on knower level classification. We conclude that the digital version may replace the physical act-out task in many contexts, with minimal impact on classification validity.

title: Humor: The Amusing Side of the Psychology of Art and Aesthetics
description: Humor was an interest of Berlyne’s new experimental aesthetics movement, but the psychology of aesthetics and humor have since drifted apart. To reunite them, we apply an aesthetics lens to some classic and modern findings in the psychology of humor, drawing parallels between humor and the broader psychology of aesthetics and the arts for aspects of the product (e.g., words, puns, and jokes), the experience (e.g., feeling amused, irritated, or embarrassed by jokes), and the audience (e.g., the massive individual differences in what people find funny). Its intrinsic interest aside, the psychology of humor reminds us of the sheer ubiquity of comic creative work and highlights the importance of amusing, playful, and lighthearted experiences of the arts.

title: The Emperor's New Diagnoses: Psychedelics, Psychosis, and the Limits of Psychiatric Distinctions
description: Psychedelic and psychotic experiences are institutionally treated as belonging to different orders — yet in phenomenology and in cultural interpretation, they often converge. The present paper examines that gap. It sets out the similarities and differences between the two — chiefly the predominance of visual rather than auditory hallucinations in psychedelic experience, the role of insight, the influence of context in both, and the asymmetry in clinical response. It does not adjudicate the causal question of whether psychedelics can induce psychosis; the clinical, population, and naturalistic literature answer different questions, and none of them closes the case. I argue, rather, that psychosis research has much to gain from attending to features long central in psychedelic science: the significance of subjective experience and meaning-making, the influence of set and setting, and the moral commitment to impartial care. The aim is narrow — to mark what the available comparison does and does not warrant — but the implications, I suggest, bear on how psychiatry frames, studies, and responds to altered states more broadly.

title: Engagement-centered demonstrations in large enrollment introductory psychology classes: effects on understanding, retention, and student engagement
description:
Background. Large enrollment introductory psychology courses often struggle with low student engagement, which can hinder learning outcomes. 

Objective. This study evaluated the effectiveness of interactive demonstrations on student engagement, short-term understanding, and long-term retention of key concepts in a large introductory course.

Method. Eight demonstrations were developed and delivered quasi-experimentally across two course sections (n = 276). Student understanding was assessed via in-class polling, and retention was measured using the same questions on the final exam. Engagement was evaluated using the Classroom Observation Protocol for Undergraduate STEM.

Results. Demonstrations significantly increased student engagement; however, linear mixed-effects models revealed no statistically significant effect on understanding or retention. 

Conclusion. Structured demonstrations increase engagement but have limited effects on test scores. Their learning effectiveness may depend on concept difficulty. 

Teaching Implications. Psychology instructors should consider incorporating interactive demonstrations into their teaching to foster engagement. Further research is warranted to better understand factors that can improve associated learning outcomes, including content complexity and demonstration style.

title: Can Multi-Task Eye-Movement Profiles Identify People Across Recording Blocks?
description:
Eye-movement biometrics are often evaluated in narrowly defined tasks, leaving open the
question of whether a broader behavioral profile can identify people more robustly across
time. We address this question by combining features from multiple eye-tracking tasks,
including grid-based viewing, smooth pursuit, microsaccades, blinks, free viewing, and
pupil responses, into one oculomotor profile per participant and recording block. We then
test whether a held-out block can be matched back to the correct participant. All three
models we evaluated identified people far above chance: a family-weighted cosine fusion
model, which learns cross-validated weights for each task family in the cross-session
benchmark, reached the numerically highest top-1 accuracy in every cohort (0.88 in the
primary Neon-only cohort and 0.79 in the EyeLink dual-setup cohort), but a subject-level
paired bootstrap showed that its advantage over a simpler unweighted cosine baseline ($0.80$
Neon; 0.71 EyeLink) was not statistically distinguishable. Feature analyses showed that
useful identity information was distributed across multiple task families---most strongly
grid and smooth-pursuit features---rather than being driven by a single measure. Because the
Neon-only and dual-setup Neon profiles come from different participant samples, a cohort
classifier separated them almost perfectly (AUC = 0.99), reflecting a combination of
recording-context and between-sample differences. These findings indicate that multi-task
oculomotor fingerprinting is feasible, but that careful attention to acquisition conditions
and to the limits of small-sample model comparisons is essential when interpreting biometric
performance.

title: The Arousal-Space Metaphor: Evidence from Spatial Mapping in a 3D Volumetric Environment
description: Spatial metaphors linking valence to physical location—such as feeling up or being down—have been extensively documented. However, valence and arousal co-vary systematically, leaving open the question of whether previously reported vertical-space effects reflect valence, arousal, or both. The present work addresses this question by having participants positioned Czech affective adjectives in a three-dimensional virtual space. Stimuli were selected via Shannon entropy to orthogonally represent valence and arousal, minimizing their usual correlation. Across three studies (data collected in 2025 and 2026), we examined spatial placement (Studies 1–2) and perceptual validation of adjective location (Study 3). Linear mixed-effects models revealed that both valence and arousal independently predicted vertical placement (Y-axis), with positive valence or high arousal being placed higher. Valence consistently predicted depth placement (Z-axis), with positive adjectives placed closer to the body and negative adjectives further away, consistent with approach-avoidance frameworks. No consistent effects emerged on the horizontal axis. Study 3 confirmed perceptual validity: congruent pairings of valence and arousal the strongest agreement judgments (e.g., OR = 122.41 for positive, high-arousal adjectives placed high), while incongruent pairings of valence and arousal (e.g., positive, low-arousal adjectives) produced uncertainty about the correct location of these adjectives. These findings demonstrate that arousal constitutes an independent contributor to vertical spatial-affective mapping—a dimension largely overlooked in prior work due to its natural covariation with valence—and that the depth axis operates primarily as a valence domain. Substantial individual differences in the application of affective-spatial metaphors were observed across all studies.

title: Assessing the efficacy of crowdsourced fact-checking for TikTok videos
description: Social media companies are increasingly shifting towards crowdsourced fact-checking approaches, which are more scalable than solely relying on professional fact-checkers. While past work suggests these approaches are effective for news headlines, it is unclear whether they are effective for short-form video content like TikToks, which are increasingly prevalent as a source of news/information. We compare the accuracy ratings of three professional fact-checkers to those of layperson crowds on three politicized topics: the Ukraine/Russia conflict, climate change, and abortion. Professional fact-checkers showed reasonable agreement on TikToks about the Ukraine/Russia conflict and abortion, but poor agreement on TikToks about climate change. Poorer performance by Republican laypeople meant that politically-balanced crowds performed as well as professional fact-checkers on Ukraine/Russia TikToks, while only Democrat-only crowds performed as well as professionals on abortion TikToks. A classifier using layperson ratings to predict professionals’ ratings performed well on TikToks where professionals’ ratings were unanimous, suggesting that crowdsourcing may be effective for unambiguously true or false TikToks.

title: Bayesian Evidence Synthesis under Heterogeneity
description: Bayesian evidence synthesis (BES) provides a way of synthesising research without pooling effects, allowing for quantitative synthesise procedures when the more traditional common-effects and random-effects models cannot be used. BES can be applied through the multiplication of independent Bayes factors assessing a common theory, quantifying the evidence for same informative hypothesis given all observed studies. This paper evaluates the behaviour of BES under varying levels of heterogeneity, and extends the methodological framework to incorporate model space inference (MSI) for more nuanced synthesis results. We do this through simulation of a standard mean difference scenario, examining how various hypothesis evaluations complement one another and provide independent information that can mitigate the potential for false positive inferences. Our results depict the high sensitivity and specificity of BES, and illustrate how heterogeneity affects BES. Our simulation results provide guidance for real world application of BES, discussing what aspects of the method to keep in mind when synthesising evidence comparing two means. In addition to this, we present an empirical example further detailing the application of the method.

title: Ethnoracial and Linguistic Diversity in Treatment Research for Primary Progressive Aphasia: A Systematic Review
description:
Purpose: This systematic review sought to characterize the ethnoracial and linguistic representation of participants in the nonpharmacological intervention literature for primary progressive aphasia (PPA) and primary progressive apraxia of speech (PPAOS). In addition, we aimed to identify which social determinants of health (SDOH) factors are most frequently reported across studies. 

Method: We performed a comprehensive search across six electronic databases: OVID Medline, OVID PsycINFO, EBSCO Medline, EBSCO CINAHL Plus, Embase, and Web of Science, as well as unpublished literature. We identified 149 original studies that administered neuromodulation and/or speech-language interventions to individuals with PPA or PPAOS and reported communication outcomes relative to a baseline or control group. From these studies, we extracted data on participants’ race, ethnicity, spoken languages, occupation, years of education, and other relevant sociodemographic variables.

Results: Ethnoracial and linguistic diversity in the current PPA literature is limited and underrepresented. Among studies that reported the extracted variables, the majority of participants were identified as non-Hispanic White, and most studies were conducted in the United States. English was the most commonly reported spoken language and was frequently used as an inclusion criterion. Regarding SDOH, participants tend to have medium-high education and hold higher skill-level occupations. Very few studies reported retirement status and whether retirement was due to symptom onset.

Conclusions: Current intervention research for PPA and PPAOS lacks ethnoracial and linguistic diversity.  This underrepresentation is further compounded by limited reporting of factors related to SDOH. title: A Narrative Review of the Role of Social Observation on Error Monitoring
description: Error monitoring is the process by which the brain self-evaluates whether responses are correct and in line with achieving task goals. The error-related negativity (ERN), a neural marker of error monitoring, is influenced by the motivational significance of errors. For example, making a mistake while being observed can be more salient than when alone. The current narrative review assesses whether error monitoring is consistently upregulated within the presence of others. Additionally, we explore the possible influence of paradigm-related factors, such as deception and feedback, and individual factors, such as age and anxiety, on relations between social observation and the ERN. We find that use of deception or feedback may increase ERN amplitudes under social observation. In contrast, presence of an authority figure and whether an observer is physically (or virtually) present do not appear to impact effects of social observation. Specific subconstructs of anxiety, such as fear of negative evaluation, may more strongly influence the ERN under social observation. We also find that the ERN increases under social observation for both youth and adults, although potentially more consistently among youth. We conclude by providing methodological recommendations and propose future directions for this burgeoning area of research.

title: Intersecting Identities and Campus Well-Being: Mental Health, Substance Use, and Service Barriers Among Racial/Ethnic and Sexual/Gender Minoritized Students at a Canadian University
description: Sexual and gender minoritized (SGM) and racial and ethnic minoritized (REM) and university students face unique minority stressors that increase risk of mental health problems and substance use. Yet, little research examines how intersecting identities influence barriers to accessing campus services. We investigated associations between these identities - including their intersections - and mental health, substance use, and obstacles to utilizing campus-based services. We conducted an online survey with 1,009 undergraduate students (Mage= 20.6, SD= 5.1) at a Canadian university about mental health symptoms and substance use, as well as experiences with and barriers to accessing campus mental health and substance use services. Regression analyses revealed few differences in mental health severity and barriers to accessing campus services between most REM subgroups and white students. Most REM subgroups reported lower rates of substance use, greater awareness of campus services, and found services more helpful relative to white students. Sexually minoritized students reported greater severity of mental health symptoms and more barriers to accessing campus services relative to heterosexual students. Interactions between SGM and REM identities did not correspond with differing outcomes. Our findings highlight the need for tailored campus services that address unique challenges faced by diverse minoritized student populations.
